bodyText:
What's happened/new
Accenture reported 4QFY26 (quarter ended Aug 31) results on October 1, with revenue of US$18.7bn, up 7% in local currency and above its guidance range, beating the street consensus. It further guides FY27 revenue growth of 3-6% in local currency, and GAAP EPS of US$14.39-14.81.

Comments
We believe AI is creating an overall "more volume, lower unit price" dynamic in consulting. Many investors had priced in a sharp hit to consulting demand from AI, and Accenture’s results show demand is holding. Accenture logged more client bookings above US$100mn in FY26 than in FY25. Management says much of current growth comes from helping clients upgrade their IT systems and data so they can use AI at scale. Over 400 clients started their first advanced AI project in FY26, and bookings with Accenture's eight emerging AI and data partners increased significantly. But there is also a trade-off in price. Management acknowledges lower pricing in many areas in 4Q, as it passes AI-driven productivity to clients at renewal and offsets this with expanded scope.

Accenture is also selling headcount to selling outcomes and assets. Fixed-price work, including outcome-based contracts, now exceeds 65% of bookings. For FY25, management put the fixed-price’s share at about 60% of its work. According to the management, Accenture's recent acquisitions aim at strategically expanding that share and breaking into high-growth areas. It spent US$4.9bn on acquisitions in FY26 and plans to spend US$5bn more in FY27. These are businesses whose revenue is not tied to headcount. Examples include Ookla, a network data and software licensing business closed in 4Q, and a majority stake in security software vendor Dragos, closed in September. Management expects to build competitive advantages by fueling organic growth in longer term with acquisitions.

Accenture's beat provides a positive read-through for enterprise AI services demand. While foundation models become more capable, enterprises still need significant human expertise to integrate AI with existing data and systems and move AI applications into production. Accelerating AI adoption could therefore create incremental demand for deployment capabilities, particularly as enterprises scale AI across more complex workflows.

Risks
Risks include slowing global economy, faster AI-driven pricing pressure, acquisition integration risks.
